topic: The Radium Girls: the glowing paint that poisoned a generation of young women
script:
In the early 1920s, in a small town in New Jersey, people would sometimes see something strange walking home at night. Young women. And they were glowing.

Their hair shimmered. Their hands gave off a soft green light. Some of them had painted their nails and even their teeth with the same paint they used at work, just for fun, because it made them shine in the dark.

They thought it was the most magical job in America. It was killing them.

This is the story of the Radium Girls, the young women who were told a deadly substance was safe, and who refused to stay quiet when they found out the truth.

To understand how this happened, we have to go back to 1898. In a cold shed in Paris, Marie and Pierre Curie discovered a new element. It glowed with its own light. It gave off heat without burning. They called it radium.

Within a few years, radium was the most exciting substance in the world. Newspapers called it a miracle. Companies sold radium face creams, radium toothpaste, radium chocolate, and bottles of radium water that promised energy and youth. People really believed that a little radioactivity was good for you.

And then came the First World War.

Soldiers in the trenches needed to read their watches and instruments in the dark. The answer was a paint made from radium mixed with glue and powder. It glowed for years. One brand was even called Undark.

In Orange, New Jersey, a company called the United States Radium Corporation opened a factory to paint those glowing dials. They hired young women, many of them still teenagers, because they had small, steady hands. The pay was excellent, better than almost any other job a working-class girl could get. The girls were proud. They were helping the war effort, and they were earning real money.

The work was delicate. Each dial had tiny numbers, and the brushes were made of fine camel hair. After a few strokes, the brush would spread out and lose its point. So the women were taught a simple trick to keep it sharp.

Lip. Dip. Paint.

Put the brush between your lips to bring it to a point. Dip it in the glowing paint. Paint the number. Then do it again. Hundreds of times a day. Every single time, they swallowed a tiny amount of radium.

Some of them asked if it was safe. They were told it was. Radium was a health product, after all. It was sold in tonics. Why would it hurt anyone?

But here's the detail that makes this story so hard to hear. In the same company, the scientists who worked directly with radium were careful. They used lead screens. They handled the material with tongs. The people at the top knew radium had to be treated with respect. The women at the painting tables were never told.

A few years later, the first workers started getting sick.

It began with their teeth. A painter named Mollie Maggia went to the dentist with a toothache. The tooth was removed, but the pain didn't stop. Then another tooth came loose. Then another. Her jaw stopped healing. Doctors had no idea what they were looking at. Mollie died in 1922. She was in her mid-twenties. Her death certificate blamed a completely different disease, one that suggested she had brought it on herself.

Then her friends started getting sick too. Pain in their hips and legs. Weakness. Bones that broke too easily. Jaws that wouldn't heal. Doctors were confused, because the symptoms didn't match anything they knew.

What was actually happening was invisible. The body treats radium a lot like calcium. So instead of passing through, it settles into the bones. And once it's there, it keeps giving off radiation, day and night, for the rest of a person's life. The women had been slowly poisoned from the inside, one brushstroke at a time.

The company's response was to deny everything. When a study it had paid for found a link between the work and the illnesses, the results were not shared honestly with the public. The company suggested the women were sick for other reasons. Some doctors who examined the workers were connected to the company itself.

But a few people started asking the right questions. A local medical examiner named Harrison Martland developed tests that could detect radioactivity in the living, and in the dead. When he examined the bodies of workers who had died, the results were impossible to deny. Their bones were radioactive.

Years later, Mollie Maggia's body was examined again. The original explanation for her death was wrong. It had been radium all along.

In 1927, five former dial painters decided to do something almost no one in their position did at the time. They sued. Grace Fryer, Edna Hussman, Katherine Schaub, and two sisters, Quinta McDonald and Albina Larice.

It was a race against time. The women were seriously ill, and the company's lawyers used every delay they could. Newspapers across the country followed the case and gave them a name that stuck: the Radium Girls. Some reporters called them the women doomed to die.

In 1928, the company settled. Each woman received ten thousand dollars, a yearly payment of six hundred dollars, and their medical bills covered. It was a victory, but a painful one. All five women died within a few years.

And the story wasn't over. Because more than eight hundred miles away, in Ottawa, Illinois, another company was still painting glowing dials. It was called the Radium Dial Company. Its workers were young women too, and they had been taught the very same technique.

As the news from New Jersey spread, the company reassured its workers. It even published a notice in the local newspaper saying that its employees were healthy and the work was safe.

They weren't, and it wasn't.

One of those women was Catherine Donohue. By the late 1930s, she was so ill she could barely walk. But she and her former coworkers took the company to court anyway. In 1938, Catherine was too sick to travel, so the hearing came to her. Lawyers and officials gathered around her bed while she gave her testimony.

The ruling went in her favor. The company appealed, again and again, all the way up the court system. Catherine died that same year. In 1939, the final appeal was rejected. The women had won.

So what did the Radium Girls actually change?

First, their cases helped establish something we now take for granted: that a company can be held responsible when its workers are harmed by the job. Before them, it was incredibly hard for a worker to prove that their illness came from their workplace. After them, the law started to change.

Second, science learned from them. For decades, researchers studied the dial painters, with many of the survivors volunteering, to understand how radioactive materials affect the human body. Those findings helped set safety limits for radiation. When thousands of scientists and workers began handling radioactive materials during the Second World War, the safety rules that protected them were built in part on what the Radium Girls had suffered.

In other words, these young women, many of them just teenagers when they started, ended up protecting people they would never meet.

Today, when you see a warning label at work, or a safety rule that seems annoying, it's worth remembering where some of those rules came from. They came from people like Grace, and Mollie, and Catherine, who were told everything was fine, and who had the courage to prove that it wasn't.

They glowed in the dark. And in a way, they still do.

If this story stayed with you, subscribe for more of the stories science history forgot. And tell me in the comments, had you ever heard of the Radium Girls before today?

youtube.description:
In the 1920s, young women painted glowing watch dials with radium paint - and were told to point their brushes with their lips.

This is the true story of the Radium Girls: how a 'miracle' element was sold as healthy, why the factory workers started getting sick while the company's own scientists wore protection, and how a group of women in their twenties took on a corporation and won - changing workplace safety and radiation science forever.

Featuring Grace Fryer, Mollie Maggia, Catherine Donohue and the women of Orange, New Jersey and Ottawa, Illinois.
